trails.bestSeason: Mar-May, Sept-Nov (avoid midday in summer heat)
trails.trailTip: There is no shade and little water on this hike — carry at least 1 liter per person and avoid midday starts in summer, when slickrock surface temperatures soar.
trails.didYouKnow: Delicate Arch stands 46 feet tall and is the most photographed arch in the park, but geologists estimate it could naturally collapse within a few centuries as erosion continues.

trails.trailTip: The Primitive Loop past Double O Arch involves narrow fins and drop-offs requiring hands-on scrambling — most hikers turn around at Double O Arch and retrace their steps instead.
trails.didYouKnow: Devils Garden passes more named arches than any other trail in the park, including Landscape Arch, at over 300 feet the longest natural stone span in North America.

trails.bestSeason: Year-round (early morning or evening in summer)
trails.trailTip: This is one of the most popular short hikes in the park — arrive early or late in the day in summer to beat both the heat and the parking crowds.
trails.didYouKnow: The North and South Windows are sometimes called the 'Spectacles' because, seen from a distance, the two openings resemble a pair of eyeglasses.

trails.trailTip: Stay on the trail and off the slope beneath the arch — a large slab fell from Landscape Arch in 1991, and the area directly underneath remains closed for safety.
trails.didYouKnow: At roughly 306 feet long, Landscape Arch is the longest natural arch in North America — its thinnest section is narrower than a school bus is long.

trails.trailTip: Arranging a car shuttle between the Park Avenue and Courthouse Towers viewpoints lets you hike one-way instead of retracing your steps.
trails.didYouKnow: Park Avenue is named for its resemblance to a canyon of skyscrapers — the towering sandstone fins were carved from a single rock layer by water working along parallel fractures.

trails.trailTip: Carry more water than you think you'll need — this route has no shade and the slickrock sections past Landscape Arch add real elevation gain on the way out.
trails.didYouKnow: Double O Arch is named for its two stacked openings, a large arch sitting directly above a smaller one, a rare formation even among the park's more than 2,000 catalogued arches.

trails.trailTip: You can walk directly through the opening of Broken Arch itself — a rare chance in the park to pass under an arch rather than just view it.
trails.didYouKnow: Broken Arch isn't actually broken — the crack across its top is a narrow fracture that hasn't yet caused the span to fail, and it may stand for a very long time.

elevationProfile.label: Loop closes near Devils Garden Campground

trails.trailTip: The route crosses soft sand washes and unmarked slickrock in places — carry a map or offline GPS track, since this corner of the park sees far fewer hikers.
trails.didYouKnow: Tower Arch sits in the Klondike Bluffs area, one of the quietest corners of Arches, named for early 20th-century guide Alexander Ringhoffer, whose reports of the area helped establish the park.

trails.bestSeason: Apr-Oct (permits sell out in peak season)
trails.trailTip: As of September 2026, NPS.gov requires either a ranger-guided hike or a self-guided exploration permit booked through Recreation.gov in advance — walk-up access isn't allowed, and permits can sell out days ahead in peak season.
trails.didYouKnow: The Fiery Furnace gets its name from the way its narrow sandstone fins glow orange-red at sunset, not from any heat — inside, the maze-like canyons stay noticeably cooler than the open desert.

animals.whereToLook: Cache Valley and the Klondike Bluffs area
animals.viewingTip: Scan distant slickrock benches with binoculars rather than expecting a close encounter — the herd is small and keeps to remote terrain.
animals.didYouKnow: Arches' bighorn sheep population was reintroduced in the 1980s after the original population was extirpated by disease and hunting in the early 20th century.

animals.whereToLook: Sunny slickrock outcrops throughout the park
animals.viewingTip: Look for a flash of bright green-blue on warm rock in the middle of the day — collared lizards are most active in full sun, unlike many desert reptiles.
animals.didYouKnow: Collared lizards can sprint on their hind legs alone, lifting their front half off the ground in a bipedal run when chasing prey or fleeing danger.

animals.whereToLook: Sandy desert flats and dens throughout the park
animals.viewingTip: Daytime sightings are very unlikely — your best chance is spotting fresh tracks in the sand in early morning. If you find a den, admire it from a distance rather than lingering or approaching it, since kit foxes will abandon a den site they perceive as disturbed.
animals.didYouKnow: Kit foxes are among the smallest fox species in North America and have oversized ears that help radiate excess body heat in the desert.

animals.whereToLook: Open desert scrub near roads and campgrounds
animals.viewingTip: Drive park roads slowly around dusk, when jackrabbits become active and are easy to spot bounding through headlight range.
animals.didYouKnow: A jackrabbit's oversized ears aren't just for hearing — they're full of blood vessels that help the animal shed heat in the desert without sweating.

animals.whereToLook: Soaring above sandstone fins and cliff faces park-wide
animals.viewingTip: Scan open sky above fins and cliff lines rather than the ground — golden eagles hunt by soaring high and stooping on rabbits and rodents below.
animals.didYouKnow: Golden eagles can spot a rabbit from over a mile away thanks to eyesight roughly four to eight times sharper than a human's.

animals.whereToLook: Campgrounds, picnic areas, and brushy desert edges
animals.viewingTip: Check shaded brush near campgrounds in early morning — cottontails rest through the heat of the day and are easiest to see in cooler hours.
animals.didYouKnow: Desert cottontails can survive without ever drinking free water, getting all the moisture they need from the plants they eat.

animals.whereToLook: High sandstone cliffs, including near Devils Garden and Park Avenue
animals.viewingTip: Look for a falcon perched on a high ledge or stooping in a steep dive near cliff faces — avoid lingering directly beneath an active nest ledge in spring.
animals.didYouKnow: Peregrine falcons were removed from the U.S. Endangered Species List in 1999 after populations rebounded from a near-collapse caused by the pesticide DDT.

animals.whereToLook: Sunny slickrock and rock crevices throughout the park
animals.viewingTip: Watch where you place your hands and feet on rock ledges, since this small rattlesnake's pale, faded coloring blends almost seamlessly into sandstone — if you spot one, give it a wide berth and let it be rather than trying to move it or get a closer look.
animals.didYouKnow: Despite its small size, the midget faded rattlesnake's venom is considered unusually potent relative to its body size compared to other rattlesnake subspecies.

animals.whereToLook: Overlooks, fins, and picnic areas throughout the park
animals.viewingTip: Keep food secured at overlooks and picnic tables — ravens are notoriously bold and intelligent, and quick to snatch an unattended snack.
animals.didYouKnow: Ravens are among the most intelligent birds known, capable of problem-solving, tool use, and remembering human faces for years.
